5 Probabilistic Risk Assessment Safety Functions, Design Criteria, and Structure,
System, and Component Classification

The Long Mott Generating Station (LMGS) preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) chapter 5,
“PRA Safety Functions, Design Criteria, and SSC Classifications,” describes the LMGS
probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) safety functions (PSFs), including required safety functions
(RSFs), and required functional design criteria (RFDC), complementary design criteria (CDC),
principal design criteria (PDC), and classification of safety-related and non-safety-related with
special treatment (NSRST) structures, systems, and components (SSCs).

LME states in PSAR chapter 5 that “[t]he Xe-100 design follows the methodology in Nuclear
Energy Institute (NEI) 18-04 as described in the Xe-100 Risk-Informed Performance-Based
Technology Inclusive Licensing Basis Development Licensing Topical Report (LTR)
(ML22187A279).” This SE chapter evaluates the consistency of LME’s methodology and results
of SSC classification with the approach outlined in NEI 18-04 and the LTR.

PSAR table 1.4-4 incorporates by reference the LTR, which the NRC approved in a safety
evaluation dated August 4, 2022 (ML22187A279). PSAR table 1.4-6 addresses the one
limitation documented in the staff's safety evaluation of this LTR (ML22187A271) by noting that
exemptions from the regulations related to LME’s implementation of the NEI 18-04 methodology
are addressed in Part V of the construction permit (CP) application.

The NRC staff evaluation of the exemption from the “safety-related SSCs’ definition under 10
CFR 50.2 and 10 CFR 26.5, and “safety-related electric equipment” defined in 10 CFR
50.49(b)(1) is documented in section 15.2 of this SE.

5.1 Safety Classification of Structures, Systems, and Components

PSAR section 5.1 describes the SSC classification methodology and categories for the LMGS
design. The SSC classification categories are safety-related (SR), non-safety-related with
special treatment (NSRST), and non-safety-related with no special treatment (NST).

PSAR section 5.2 provides a high-level description of the PSFs that were identified as SR (also
referred to as RSFs) and NSRST through the NEI 18-04 process. PSAR section 5.4 provides
the selection of the SR SSCs performing RSFs and PSAR section 5.5 provides the selection of
NSRST SSCs to perform NSRST PSFs. PSAR chapters 6 and 7 provide additional details on
the criteria and capabilities of safety-significant SSCs, i.e., those classified as SR and NSRST.

The applicable regulatory requirements for the evaluation of SSC classification are as follows:

e 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1),
e 10 CFR 50.34(a)(4)

 The applicable guidance for SSC classification is as follows:

e RG 1.233, “Guidance for a Technology Inclusive, Risk-Informed, and Performance-
Based Methodology to Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for
Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” (ML20091L698)
which endorses NEI 18-04, “Risk-Informed Performance-Based Technology Inclusive
Guidance for Non-Light Water Reactor Licensing Basis Development,” Revision 1
(ML19241A472), with clarifications.

e RG 1.253, “Guidance for a Technology-Inclusive Content-of-Application Methodology to
Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for Licenses, Certifications, and
Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” (ML23269A222) which endorses NEI 21-07,
“Technology Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light Water Reactors, Safety Analysis Report
Content: For Applicants Using the NEI 18-04 Methodology,” Revision 1 (ML22060A190),
with clarifications and additions.

The regulations in 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1) and (4) together require that each CP applicant submit in
its PSAR a safety assessment with a preliminary analysis and evaluation of the design and
performance of facility SSCs. Specifically, 10 CFR 50.34(a)(1)(ii)(D) requires consideration be
given to the safety features that are to be engineered into the facility and those barriers that
must be breached as a result of an accident before a release of radioactive material to the
environment can occur. Special attention must be directed to plant design features intended to
mitigate the radiological consequences of accidents. The requirements of 10 CFR 50.34(a)(4)
specify that the objective of the preliminary analysis and evaluation of the design and
performance of SSCs is to assess the risk to public health and safety resulting from operation of
the facility, including determination of the margins of safety during normal operations and
transient conditions during the life of the facility, and the adequacy of SSCs provided for the
prevention of accidents and mitigation of consequences of accidents. These required
assessments of the facility provide an understanding of those SSCs that are most important to
radiological health and safety because they play a key role in preventing and mitigating
accidents. The regulations in 10 CFR Part 50 establish that certain SSCs are SR (as defined in
10 CFR 50.2) and require applicants and licensees to design, fabricate, construct, and test
those SSCs in accordance with standards, quality requirements, etc., beyond those applied in
normal industrial practice to commercial grade SSCs as necessary to ensure their reliability and
capability to prevent and mitigate accidents; other requirements may apply to SSCs that are
safety-significant but not SR.

The guidance in NEI 18-04, as endorsed with clarifications in RG 1.233, provides an acceptable
process for using the PRA and licensing basis event (LBE) analyses to classify an SSC based
on the role it plays in prevention and mitigation of LBEs, as described in more detail in chapter 3
of the PSAR and this SE. Under this process, the most safety-significant SSCs are classified as
SR, SSCs that perform safety-significant functions but are less safety-significant are classified
as NSRST, and other SSCs are classified as NST. These classifications are an integral part of
the licensing basis development process described in NEI 18-04, because they are used to
assess SSCs according to their safety- or risk-significance and identify if special treatments
beyond normal industrial practices are needed to ensure SSC performance of safety functions
in the prevention and mitigation of LBEs.

5.1.1. Technical Evaluation

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 5.1 to determine if the SSC classification methodology
and categories conform to the relevant guidance in RG 1.233 and RG 1.253. The NRC staff also
held audit discussions focused on LME’s implementation of the methodology described in the
PSAR to confirm that it is consistent with the NEI 18-04 methodology and the RGs, as
documented in the General Audit Report (ML...).

During its review of the PSAR, the NRC staff identified certain areas of the NEI 18-04 guidance
and corresponding endorsement in RG 1.233 that were interpreted differently by LME and the
NRC staff. Through audit discussions, understanding was reached on these differing
interpretations and how they may have impacted the SSC safety classifications provided in the
PSAR. In areas where LME had unintentionally deviated from the licensing modernization
project (LMP) methodology, LME implemented changes to its process to align more closely with
the LMP methodology. One such area was captured in the staffs request for confirmation of
information (RCI)-1 dated August 14, 2026 (ML26230A155) and in the evaluation below.

RCI-1 documents preliminary results of the risk-significance evaluation steps that were
inadvertently not performed by LME. As confirmed through RCI-1, these results are not
incorporated into Rev 1 of the PSAR, but at the time of this SE are in the process of being
incorporated into the safety analysis and design. The NRC staff has documented areas where
the design and special treatments are expected to change based on these preliminary results
and confirmation of final risk-significance determinations and appropriate treatment within the
design will be performed at the OL. The PSAR currently includes results that are inconsistent
with the results application of the methodology as revised in RCI-1 (see Table 5.1-2 below).
Application of the methodology described in RCI-1 will yield different results, as described
below, based on corrections to the methodology. To the extent use of the corrected
methodology provides confidence that the final risk-significance determinations will be
satisfactory, that information will be available for the operating license (OL) application and the
staff will review it in the context of the OL application..

The NRC staff reviewed PSAR section 1.3.1, which states that the applicant follows the overall
NEI 18-04 methodology, as endorsed in RG 1.233, and PSAR section 5.1.1, which states that
LME follows the risk-informed and performance-based methodology in RG 1.233. Classification
of SSCs is a key component of the NEI 18-04 methodology and based, in part, on the safety
functions the SSC performs and the SSC’s safety significance. LME describes a systematic
and iterative process for selection of LBEs, classification of SSCs, and determination of
defense-in-depth (DID) adequacy. As described in PSAR section 5.1.1, LME follows the
guidance in RG 1.233 with some departures in the classification of essential support SSCs as
discussed below.

Consistent with the guidance in RG 1.233, LME uses the following SSC classification
categories:

+ Safety-related:

- SSCs selected by the designer from the SSCs that are available to perform the RSFs to
mitigate the consequences of design basis events (DBEs) to within the LBE Frequency-
Consequence (F-C) Target, and to mitigate design basis accidents (DBAs) that only rely
on the SR SSCs to meet the dose limits of 10 CFR 50.34 using conservative
assumptions

- SSCs selected by the designer and relied on to perform RSFs to prevent the frequency
of beyond design basis events (BDBEs) with consequences greater than the 10 CFR
50.34 dose limits from increasing into the DBE region and beyond the F-C Target

+ Non-safety-related with special treatment (NSRST):

- Non-safety-related SSCs relied on to perform risk-significant functions. Risk-significant
SSCs are those that perform functions that prevent or mitigate any LBE from exceeding
the F-C Target or make significant contributions to the cumulative risk metrics selected
for evaluating the total risk from all analyzed LBEs.

- Non-safety-related SSCs relied on to perform functions requiring special treatment for
DID adequacy

+ Non-safety-related with no special treatment (NST)
- All other SSCs (with no special treatment required)

Table 5.1-1 of this SE summarizes the six evaluation steps in the NEI 18-04 SSC methodology
that are used in determining what SSCs fall into each of the SSC categories. The first five
evaluation tasks are quantitative steps performed using the PRA. The final step, the DID
evaluation, is a qualitative step that assesses the layers of safety in the design and ensures the
SSC classification is risk-informed. The DID evaluation is described in PSAR section 4.2 and
evaluated in section 4.2 of this SE.

During its review, NRC staff determined that LME’s SSC classification methodology was
inconsistent with the NEI 18-04 methodology as listed below. As described in the evaluation that
follows, the NRC staff evaluated the safety impact of these inconsistencies at the CP application
stage. For tasks 7a.1 and 7a.2, the PSAR results are consistent or conservative with what
would have resulted from following the NEI 18-04 methodology. For tasks 7a.3 and 7b, LME
confirmed via RCI-01 changes to its evaluation that will be implemented but were not
incorporated into the PSAR.

e LME assumed failure of all non-safety related SSCs instead of assessing the impact of
individual functions or SSCs and did not include BDBEs with frequency bands extending
into the DBE region in the evaluation for task 7a.1 of table 5.1-1 of this SE.

e LME did not define the process for evaluating BDBEs that exceeded the 10 CFR 50.34
dose limits (i.e., high-consequence BDBEs) to assess which SSCs were relied on to
maintain LBEs below the F-C target as described in task 7a.2 of table 5.1-1 of this SE.

e LME did not perform task 7a.3 in Table 5.1-1 of this SE, but the evaluation performed in
lieu of task 7a.1 might have assigned a SR classification to some of the impacted SSCs
and others were assigned NSRST for DID under step 7e.

e LME’s evaluation did not assume failure of the function or SSC and then evaluate the
impact on the cumulative risk metrics as described in task 7b of Table 5.1-1 of this SE.

e LME identified an alternative approach for the classification of some load path SSCs for
SSCs performing SR functions from that in RG 1.233, staff position C.2.a. Load path
SSCs for SSCs performing some SR functions are classified as risk-significant NSRST.

Task 7a.1

Instead of performing evaluations for individual function or SSC impacts on LBEs, LME
performed an evaluation that assumed failure of all non-safety-related (i.e., NSRST and NST)
SSCs and showed that no AOOs or DBEs exceeded the F-C target at 95" percentile frequency
and consequence. The NRC staff determined that LME’s evaluation produces results generally
expected to be conservative compared to the task 7a.1 evaluation because of the use of the
95" percentile instead of the mean and the evaluation of all AOOs instead of only those AOOs
that extend into the DBE region. However, because BDBEs with 95" percentiles extending into
the DBE region were not included in the evaluation, it is possible, though unlikely, that this
preliminary classification process did not identify an RSF that would have been identified with
the inclusion of these BDBEs.

The NRC staff also determined that because all functions and SSCs were evaluated together,
the risk insights that are gained through the individual function or SSCs evaluations were not
available. The NRC staff determined it to be acceptable that these risk insights are not available
at the CP stage because the generally conservative approach taken to identify SR SSCs and
the approach to identify DID NSRST SSCs (discussed below and in section 4.2 of this SE) are
unlikely to miss risk insights that would necessitate design changes. Additionally, LME has
made corrections to its methodology to perform these evaluations as confirmed in the response
to RCI-1 and will incorporate these risk insights in its design.

Task 7a.2

For task 7a.2, LME did not identify any BDBEs within the preliminary set of LBEs that exceeded
to 10 CFR 50.34 dose limits, referred to as high-consequence BDBEs by NEI 18-04. Because
there were no high-consequence BDBEs, not having the evaluation against the F-C target
defined within the process did not impact the results of the preliminary SSC classification. As
the PRA is expanded beyond full power operation core events, the LBE set may include high-
consequence BDBEs; LME has updated its methodology to ensure the impact of failed functions
or SSCs on these LBEs is evaluated consistent with the NEI 18-04 methodology and the
description of SR SSCs in PSAR section 5.1. The staff has accordingly determined that the
updated methodology is adequate to identify SR SSCs from these high-consequence BDBEs.

Task 7a.3

The NRC staff review of the evaluation of AOOs and DBEs described under Task 7a.1 above
would have assigned a classification of SR instead of NSRST to SSCs where the modeled
failure of the SSC would cause the AOO or DBE results to exceed the F-C target at the 95"
percentile, but not at the mean. The NEI 18-04 methodology indicates that these SSCs can be
classified as risk-significant NSRST. The risk-significance information to determine if any SSCs
were conservatively assigned SR instead of risk-significant NSRST through this process was
not available at the CP stage because, as noted above, LME did not perform an evaluation to
determine the impacts of individual function or SSC failing on the LBEs in support of the PSAR.
However, during the review, LME updated its SSC classification methodology to include these
evaluations and performed a preliminary evaluation that included an assessment of BDBEs that

were not covered by the 7a.1 evaluation. LME described the preliminary results of this
evaluation in the response to RCI-1 dated August 28, 2026 (ML26239A157). The applicant's
preliminary evaluation identified 14 risk-significant systems that keep LBEs below the F-C
target. Table 5.1-2 of this SE provides this list of risk-significant systems. Thirteen (13) of these
14 SSCs identified in the preliminary list of risk-significant SSCs are already being identified as
SR or NSRST within the PSAR. The remaining system, the conventional island electrical
system, that is currently classified as NST in Rev. 1 of the PSAR but included in the preliminary
list has a reasonable likelihood of being classified NST with further refinement of the PRA and
design, as discussed in more detail in sections 5.2 and 5.5 of this SE. Table 5.1-2 also includes
the impact on the other system classifications and the sections of the SE where the aspects of
the systems and their functions are further evaluated.

Task 7b

An area of NEI 18-04 that was interpreted differently by LME and the staff was the evaluation
against the cumulative risk targets, task 7b. Key statements from NEI 18-04 relating to this
evaluation include:

e “In this task, the integrated risk of all the LBEs, is evaluated against three cumulative risk
targets... One element of this task is to identify design features that are responsible for
preventing and mitigating radiological releases and for meeting the integrated risk
criteria.”

e “SSCs are classified as risk-significant if the SSC function is necessary to keep any
LBEs inside the F-C Target, or if the total frequency of LBEs with the SSCs failed is
within 1% of any of the three cumulative risk targets identified in Task 7b.”

e “This approach to assigning risk significance uses the concept of evaluating the impact
of the SSC function on the ability to meet the F-C Target, and also includes criteria
based on risk significance metrics for the cumulative risk impacts of SSC functions
across all the LBEs.“

e “The safety classification process and the corresponding special treatments serve to
control the frequencies and consequences of the LBEs within the F-C Target and to
ensure that the cumulative risk targets are not exceeded.”

The NRC staff's understanding is that this evaluation is to be performed similar to the LBE
evaluation, by first assuming failure of the function or SSC and then evaluating the impact on
the cumulative risk metrics. The staff understanding is based on the passages above, which
indicate that the purpose of the evaluation is to measure the function or SSC’s role in
maintaining cumulative risk within the target and that the cumulative risk evaluation is similar to
the LBE evaluation but looking across all LBEs.

LME’s interpretation of this evaluation is that no additional failures should be taken, and the
frequency metric used should be the total frequency for all LBEs where the SSC was already
failed in the baseline model. This approach, however, measures something different than the
LBE evaluation; it does not measure how important the function or SSC is in keeping the
cumulative risk within the F-C target, but rather measures the baseline contribution to the
cumulative risk. The applicant’s approach identifies where additional margin to cumulative risk
could be gained if the failure frequency were reduced rather than cumulative contribution to
keeping LBEs below the F-C target.

Following extensive discussion in audit, LME adjusted its SSC classification methodology to add
a step in assessing a function or an SSC’s impact on the cumulative risk metrics. This step is
confirmed in the response to RCI-1 and includes setting the failure probability for each function
or SSC to 1.0 and then comparing the results to 100% of each of the cumulative risk metrics.
When one or more of the cumulative risk metrics are exceeded, the function or SSC will be
identified as a significant risk contributor. This will not automatically change the classification,
but the information will be provided to the integrated decision-making process panel (IDPP) to
determine whether the classification should be adjusted. This assessment is performed to meet
the non-LWR PRA Standard Table 1.9-2, but LME included the review of this information by the
IDPP as part of its formal process to address the difference in interpretation for a function or
SSC’s impact on the cumulative risk metrics.

The staff determined this approach to be acceptable because it provides a reasonable way of
assessing the role an SSC plays in maintaining cumulative risk within the target.. As discussed
above, the staff conclusion has two bases. First, LME adjusted the methodology to be
consistent with the guidance in NEI-18-04, as endorsed in RG 1.233, which provides confidence
that the final risk-significance determinations will be satisfactory. Second, preliminary application
of the adjusted methodology does not change the results for 13 out of 14 systems and indicates
that the status of the 14" system, the conventional island electrical system, currently identified
as NST, will not likely change. The staff will review the final results of both cumulative risk
evaluations in the OL application.

Task 7d

Another difference between LME’s preliminary methodology and NEI 18-04 that was identified
during the review was in the assessment of LBEs in different LBE categories based on their
uncertainty bands. While LBEs are generally categorized based on their mean frequency, the
methodology in NEI 18-04 indicates that if the uncertainty band straddles a frequency boundary
that the LBE be evaluated in both categories. This impacts the LBE evaluations for the
identification of RSFs, as discussed above, and the identification and evaluation of DBAs. In
addition to identifying DBAs for DBEs, DBAs should also be identified for AOOs and BDBEs
with frequency bands that extend into the DBE region, potentially leading to additional RSFs
being identified. Because Rev. 0 of the PSAR did not include these additional events, when
LME performed the mapping of these additional events to DBAs some events did not have a
corresponding DBA and were mapped to the seismic event. This is acceptable for the CP stage
as the dose would bound the appropriate DBAs for these events and the RSFs are assessed
through the full scope of DBA analyses.

LME added the mapping of these events to DBAs in Rev. 1 of the PSAR. In the process, LME
identified two potential impacts to the design. First, LME identified SSGTL-29, a steam
generator tube leak with concurrent failure of the steam generator isolation valves, as not being
bounded by the current DBAs and having a potentially unacceptable volume of water entering
the reactor. LME addressed this by removing some of the conservatism from the frequency of
the initiating event for this LBE within the PRA. The staff finds this to be reasonable based on
the data for steam generator tube failure discussed in PSAR section 6.4.12 and the wide
uncertainty bands used. LME identified a second impact related to pressure relief on the steam
generator, where the open function was upgraded to SR because of one of the steam generator
tube rupture events being mapped to a DBA. Both LME’s implementation of the NEI 18-04

During the reevaluation of DBA mapping, LME identified some LBEs where the DBA with a
similar event sequence was not bounding due to the failure of a SR SSCs as part of the DBE or
BDBE. For the CP application, LME has mapped these events to the seismic DBA, which NRC

RG 1.233, staff position C.2.a
LME describes its approach for classification of some load path SSCs in PSAR section 5.1.1. As

stated in RG 1.233 staff position C.2.a, “The staff expects that SSCs that provide essential
support (including required human actions) for SR or NSRST SSCs will be classified in a
manner consistent with the higher-level function, even if the supporting SSC is not explicitly
modeled in the PRA.” This includes SSCs that provide a load path for SSCs performing a
safety-significant function.

PSAR section 5.1.1 describes an alternative approach for classification of load path SSCs
providing essential support. This alternative approach is applied to SSCs that do not perform
other safety-significant functions and does not include SSCs that contribute to RSF 1.4,
“Maintain Geometry” which are classified as SR based on their contribution to performing this
SR function. However, LME classifies other load path SSCs providing structural support for
SSCs performing SR functions as risk-significant NSRST.

Overall SSC Classification Methodology

The SSC classification in the PSAR is based on the preliminary LMGS design and associated
LMP process implementation including the PRA discussed in PSAR section 3.1.1. LME
committed to follow the methodology described above, which is based on the LMP process in
NEI 18-04 and RG 1.233, and the NRC staff will review the finalized SSC classification
described in the OL application when the LMGS design is mature and the LMP process is
complete. As discussed in section 3.1.4 of this SE, there were limited consequence analysis
results generated by LME for use in the PSAR. This is expected at the CP stage, but impacts
the completeness of the SSC classification. For example, when looking at initiating event
families, it is expected that each subsequent failure within an initiating family set following a
release would result in increased consequences, because the conclusion otherwise is that the
function or SSC has no mitigative impact. However, with approximately 30 unique consequence
results and over 280 events, there are many subsequent failures within the LME LBE set where
the impacts are unknown because unique consequence results were unavailable. As explained
in section 3.1.4 of this SE, the same bounding consequences were assigned to multiple LBEs
within the set, which is adequate for a CP application.

As stated in section 3.2 of the PSAR and discussed in section 3.2 of this SE, LME did not
perform the LBE family grouping step described in NEI 18-04. The family grouping step
identifies the LBEs where an SSC has little or no impact on the likelihood of an event occurring
or the mitigation of that event and provides for grouping those LBEs into a family such that they
are represented by the LBE family and not modeled as a unique event within the LBE set. While
modeling of individual LBEs without family groupings makes safety classification steps more
challenging, it is not required to determine appropriate safety classification of SSCs. Therefore,
the omission of the family grouping step is acceptable at the CP stage. LME states in PSAR
section 3.2.4 that they will perform the family grouping step in determining the final LBE set for
the OL application. As stated in section 3.1.4 of the PSAR and discussed in section 3.1.4 of this
SE, for the final set of LBEs, LME will provide a unique source term in the FSAR to demonstrate
each function’s or SSC’s impact on event frequency and consequence.

Based on its review as described above, the NRC staff finds that LME’s process for establishing
the set of LBEs and classifying SSCs follows the risk-informed and performance-based
methodology in RG 1.233 with the few exceptions evaluated above, all of which the staff
determined to be acceptable. Accordingly, the NRC staff finds that the SSC safety classification
categories are consistent with RG 1.233. . The NRC staff has determined that the level of detail
provided in the applicant's PSAR is consistent with the guidance in NEI 21-07, as endorsed with
clarifications in RG 1.253, given the preliminary design at the CP stage.

SSCs will continue as the design matures and the implementation of the systematic and

5.1.2. Conclusion

Based on the considerations described above, the NRC staff finds that the SSC classification
categories and process described in PSAR section 5.1 is consistent with the applicable
regulatory guidance with the limited exceptions evaluated above and determined to be

acceptable and, therefore, meets the regulatory requirements in 10 CFR 50.34 identified above
for the issuance of a CP in accordance with 10 CFR 50.35.

The NRC staff review of LMGS approach to defining RSFs identified that the structure of the

all other functions supporting it is reasonable for a TRISO fueled system because the functional
containment is inherent to the fuel. For a TRISO fueled system, the potential failure modes of
that functional containment are tied to the FSFs of controlling heat generation and controlling
heat removal, and the LMGS RSFs reflect those facts. Further, the reactor-specific RSFs
address the remaining two identified failure modes, with oxidation related failure being
addressed by RSF 1.3 and mechanical failure being addressed by RSF 1.4.

As the PRA is expanded to include the control of radiation from processes outside the core, the
applicant may identify additional radionuclide retention PSFs. The NRC staff has nonetheless
determined that the source terms that exist outside of the fuel would be limited compared to the
source term from the fuel. Accordingly, the staff concludes that it is unlikely that additional
PSFs would be identified as RSFs for source terms outside the core and the supplementary
evaluations described in PSAR section 3.10 and evaluated in section 3.10 of this SE and the
RSFs for radionuclide retention are adequate for the PSAR. The potential need for additional
safety-significant radionuclide retention PSFs will be evaluated at the OL application stage when
design and safety information for non-fuel sources is available.

An additional aspect of the LMGS design that impacts the RSFs is the use of inherent reactivity
feedback as one of the two independent shutdown mechanisms and identification of inherent
reactivity feedback as an RSF relied on to maintain safety. Due to its importance to safety, the
NRC staff reviewed how the effectiveness of this RSF, which is under the control heat
generation FSF, depends on the presence of high temperature, effectively creating a competing
safety priority to the control heat removal RSF. As a result, as the reactor becomes more
effective in the heat removal RSF, it becomes less effective in inherent reactivity and the control
of heat generation RSF. Because of these competing RSFs, biasing parameters to the limiting
value in one direction will not necessarily achieve a conservative result and NRC staff discussed
with the applicant that a more extensive transient analysis is needed to ensure that the range of
potential conditions, including the impacts of uncertainties, have been evaluated.

Results in PSAR section 3.6 show the depressurized loss of forced cooling (DLOFC) event as
bounding with respect to peak fuel temperature. The DLOFC event minimizes heat removal but
would have stronger negative reactivity feedback as a result, when compared with other DBAs.
To support confirming minimization of heat removal would result in bounding peak fuel
temperature, considering the competing RSFs, the NRC staff reviewed a preliminary transient
analysis in audit. The preliminary transient analyses performed by LME, supported LME’s
position that the bounding fuel temperatures will occur when heat removal is most limiting. LME
will evaluate the full range of key reactivity and thermal-hydraulic parameters across a range of
cooling conditions to ensure that the events analyzed in the FSAR represent the worst-case or
95" percentile with adequate margin maintained for both safety functions. PSAR section 3.1.7
describes the analysis that will be completed to support the OL application.

PSAR table 5.2-1 lists the required functional design criteria (RFDCs) corresponding to the
RSFs. The RFDCs are evaluated in section 5.3 and chapters 6 and 7 of the SE.
